title: Indian-Led Team Finds First Galaxy Whose Black Hole Fired Jets Four Separate Times
excerpt: Astronomers led by IISER Pune's Pavan Vijay Khadekar have identified J023721.13-010528.5 as the first known 'quadruple-double' radio galaxy, with four distinct episodes of jet activity recorded in its radio structures.
body:
• A team led by Pavan Vijay Khadekar of IISER Pune has found the first known galaxy whose central black hole launched powerful jets in four separate episodes.
  • The galaxy, J023721.13-010528.5, shows four pairs of radio hotspots with spectral ages from 4.5 to 20.5 million years, growing older with distance from the core.
  • A statistical test found the four-episode explanation about 3 million times more likely than the alternative of random knots in a single jet.
  • The S-shaped structure spans about 3.9 million light-years, making it the second-largest S-shaped radio source known.

Astronomers led by Pavan Vijay Khadekar of the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) Pune have identified what appears to be the first example of a new class of radio galaxy — one whose central supermassive black hole switched its jets on four separate times. The findings, reported by Phys.org and published in The Astrophysical Journal, are based on observations from India's upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT) combined with data from South Africa's MeerKAT and the US Very Large Array.

Four bursts, written in radio light

Radio galaxies are powered by supermassive black holes that fire jets of particles into space. Where those jets slam into surrounding gas, they create bright "hotspots." In a small subset of galaxies the black hole restarts its jets more than once, and each episode leaves its own pair of hotspots, with older pairs sitting farther from the core. Galaxies with two episodes are called double-double radio galaxies — about 192 are known. Three-episode systems are far rarer, with only seven known or candidate examples. Until now, no galaxy had been confirmed with four.

How the team proved the episodes are real

Studying the radio source J023721.13-010528.5, hosted by a massive elliptical galaxy at redshift 0.372, the team identified four distinct hotspot pairs, labelled N1–N4 and S1–S4. Their spectral ages range from 4.5 to 20.5 million years and increase steadily with distance from the core — the pattern expected from sequential outbursts, not from random knots in one continuous jet. A statistical symmetry test found the four-episode explanation roughly 3 million times more likely than the knots model. The researchers have named the class a "quadruple-double radio galaxy," or QDRG.

"We conclude that J023721.13−010528.5 exhibits four distinct episodes of jet activity, i.e., a quadruple-double radio galaxy (QDRG)."

— Khadekar et al., The Astrophysical Journal

A wobbling black hole

The axes of the successive hotspot pairs rotate counterclockwise by growing amounts — about 7, 16 and 24 degrees — suggesting the black hole's spin axis is slowly wobbling over time. That progressive rotation fits the galaxy's S-shaped form, which stretches roughly 3.9 million light-years across and is the second-largest S-shaped radio source known. The team, which also drew on researchers associated with the National Centre for Radio Astrophysics (NCRA-TIFR), argues that giant S-shaped galaxies may be the best hunting ground for more multi-episode systems.

Why it matters

Each restarted jet is a fossil record of how a black hole feeds, stalls and feeds again over tens of millions of years. A four-episode system gives astronomers an unusually complete timeline of that cycle in a single object, and a test case for models of how black holes and their host galaxies shape each other. The discovery also showcases the uGMRT near Pune, one of the world's most sensitive low-frequency radio telescopes, at the centre of a result built from three continents of instruments.
